title: Below the leaves: Integrating above‐ and below‐ground phenology for earth‐system predictability
content:
Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.


Abstract

Almost every aspect of biological systems has phenology—a pattern in activity or function linked to annual cycles. Most terrestrial phenology research focusses on leaves, the onset of leaf out or senescence. This is the easiest to measure and the most obvious form of phenology. Nonetheless, leaves are far from the only aspect of terrestrial systems with seasonal dynamics. Seasonal patterns both above- and below-ground across varying traits and organs matter for global cycles of water, carbon and other nutrients as well as the interactions between species. Through plasticity in resource allocation and trophic interactions, phenological events are not always synchronous, but do have dependencies between different organs and organisms, above- and below-ground. However, patterns across functional traits, organs and organisms are harder to parameterise than leaf phenology and so are represented more abstractly in vegetation components of land surface models used to predict the future planet. In this perspective, we ask the following: What do we know about the whole system phenology of plants and soil heterotrophs, and how are these coupled together? Can we make predictions about this coupling of phenology and its flexibility through traits, their interactions and environmental characteristics? How can these couplings best be tested under real environmental conditions? We challenge the field to generate data that allows for predictions about whole system phenological coupling and decoupling on our changing planet.
